items.summary:
Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia chief sent shockwaves through Asian markets, which have become deeply dependent on the chipmaker for their artificial intelligence industries.

Taiwan relies heavily on Nvidia because it outsources most of its chip production to TSMC; Taiwan's real economic growth since 2024 has been driven by a surge in AI-related exports. Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan as part of building the firm's planned headquarters there.

South Korea and Japan are also exposed, supplying key components such as memory chips through firms like Samsung and SK Hynix while making Nvidia's processors.

The Asia-Pacific data centre market powered largely by Nvidia is booming, with investment reaching a record $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025 according to CBRE. Google, Microsoft and Oracle also plan to boost their regional infrastructure spending by roughly 60% this year.

The Huang episode has prompted questions about how effectively Taiwan has built a 'non-China' semiconductor supply chain and how the region should manage its heavy reliance on Nvidia.

US export restrictions have renewed pressure, with Washington announcing new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. These measures restrict both high-end chip exports to China and Chinese firms' access to computing power rented abroad for AI training.

Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region according to the Financial Times, though it is unclear whether this reflects only a temporary move while the company figures out how to comply with the new rules. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.
items.title: Asia's AI boom leaves economies exposed to Nvidia and Jensen Huang

items.summary:
IBM has decided to stop sponsoring work visas and green cards for most roles in IBM Consulting, the company's largest business unit. The decision affects employees who rely on employer sponsorship to maintain their US work status or pursue permanent residency.

Affected staff have reportedly been given three weeks to decide whether to accept relocation opportunities outside the United States. Those unwilling to move will be offered three months' severance and Dec 31, 2026, as their last working day.

IBM attributes the change to evolving business requirements and shifting availability of skilled workers, noting that its reliance on US high-skilled visa programs has declined over time. The company previously used such visas to address talent shortages but gradually reduced them.
items.title: IBM ends H-1B and green card sponsorship in its consulting division

items.summary:
Japan's largest power generator JERA has begun talks with US tech companies including Anthropic and Meta to build data centres near power plants in the Tokyo area, according to a report by Nikkei on Friday.

The energy group is also discussing deals with Amazon, Microsoft and Google, per an interview with JERA Global CEO and Chair Yukio Kani reported by Nikkei. The tech companies did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

JERA previously announced in October a partnership with Dell Technologies and UK-based AI infrastructure developer RHAELM to accelerate artificial intelligence development in Japan. Under the memorandum of understanding, the partners agreed to develop a standardised model for building AI infrastructure nationally, beginning with a $15 billion hyperscale data centre in Chiba near Tokyo.

A JERA spokesperson said RHAELM handles marketing and had been told it is in talks with multiple hyperscalers. RHAELM was not immediately available for comment.
items.title: JERA Enters Talks With Anthropic, Meta Over Tokyo Data Centres

items.summary:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on 23 November after he had stepped down just 11 days earlier, joining a small group of tech founders who lost the top job and regained it.

The Nvidia board voted unanimously to bring Huang back; six days before that reversal it said it had no plans to reinstate him. The board cited an independent-director investigation into reports that foreign intelligence targeted Huang, and chair Harvey Jones called him 'the right person to lead NVIDIA.'

OpenAI's Sam Altman was removed as CEO on 17 November 2023 after the board said it lost confidence in him, then returned within two weeks when OpenAI agreed on 22 November and he officially came back on 29 November with a new board.

More than 740 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter demanding Altman return, and Microsoft offered to give him a new AI research team to lead. The article attributes these details to reporting around the episode rather than stating them as confirmed facts from OpenAI itself.

Steve Jobs lost an Apple power struggle in 1985, then returned after Apple bought his NeXT company on 20 December 1996; he became interim CEO on 16 September 1997 and later led the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad launches.

Jack Dorsey was pushed out of Twitter in October 2008 while building Square, returned as interim CEO in July 2015, became permanent CEO on 5 October 2015 still running Square, and stepped down again in 2021.

Automattic founder Matt Mullenweg was put on leave by its board on 9 September 2026 with CFO Mark Davies set to become interim CEO. The article reports that Mullenweg holds about 84% of the voting power and used it to retake control, dismiss Davies, install a new board, and said he was away for 33 hours and 20 minutes.

Each comeback had a different lever: Huang's came with an open investigation into foreign-intelligence targeting that he has agreed to cooperate with; Altman's followed employee pressure and Microsoft support; Jobs' followed Apple buying NeXT; Dorsey's followed his parallel payments business; Mullenweg's followed his dominant voting stake.
items.title: Tech founders who resigned then returned to lead

items.summary:
President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that he believes Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang poses no security threat. He said, 'I think he's absolutely fine,' while speaking at his Mar-a-Lago estate.

When asked by AFP how he could be certain given the Justice Department had not conducted an investigation into Huang, Trump said his conclusion rested on 'information I have, which is a lot of information.'
items.title: Trump Says Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Is Not a Security Threat

items.summary:
Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said on Nov 27 that ASEAN must counter rising economic nationalism through deeper integration and wider partnerships, arguing that raising barriers among member states would narrow opportunities while a more integrated bloc strengthens its value as a partner. Speaking at SPH Media's Asia Future Summit 2026 in Singapore, the Deputy Prime Minister—who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry—said broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan identified three factors that make integration especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks, and geo-economic contestation. He said each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward while simultaneously making cooperation more crucial. His remarks came after the United States announced fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves Gan noted affected many in Southeast Asia as the region sits amid sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

The Deputy Prime Minister said ASEAN countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences but can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment, and cooperation. He added that this would require earning partners' confidence through clear and predictable rules, upholding laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing as scrutiny of international trade intensifies.

Gan noted ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027 while Singapore takes on the rotating chairmanship amid heightened geopolitical contestation. He said both the United States and China would remain key economic partners given their importance to regional growth, noting they are among the region's largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

The Deputy Prime Minister also highlighted efforts to strengthen ties with other partners to expand ASEAN's economic options and reduce exposure to disruptions. These include negotiations to upgrade trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Gan pointed to recent steps strengthening integration within ASEAN that would help firms tap regional suppliers and customers. An upgraded ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement set for rollout at end-2026 will streamline procedures and improve transparency to reduce costs, while a customs mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances across participating countries. He also cited a Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month that he said makes cross-border transactions, payments, and access to digital services easier.

The Deputy Prime Minister concluded that these measures make ASEAN more valuable as a place to produce and market goods, forming a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to engage the world with greater confidence.
items.title: Gan Calls for Deeper ASEAN Integration Amid Economic Nationalism

items.summary:
Pablo Hernández de Cos, a Spanish economist, is expected to become the next president of the European Central Bank. He will succeed Christine Lagarde after she departs in February.

De Cos takes over as the eurozone faces surging inflation, sluggish growth, and rising government debt. Inflation climbed to a three-year high in October.

He will confront France's fiscal crisis two months before its presidential election. Both frontrunners, far-right leader Marine Le Pen and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, have criticized the ECB and urged policymakers to lower France's borrowing costs.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez welcomed De Cos as Spain's first ECB chief, pointing to 'a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before.'
items.title: Spanish policymaker Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead the European Central Bank

items.summary:
Singapore's incoming ASEAN chairmanship in 2027 can improve the circumstances under which it makes strategic choices, but cannot supply the capabilities that make those choices possible. ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute director Ng Chee Khern argues this distinction shapes where Singapore should invest and what to expect from the bloc.

ASEAN's main value is preserving peace among neighbours by making law and negotiation the usual way members settle disputes, keeping regional order inclusive so no member must choose a side between America and China, and giving each member more weight than it would have alone. Southeast Asia drew about US$244 billion of foreign direct investment inflows in 2025 against US$105 billion for China, which gives the great powers reason to seek cooperation through benefits rather than pressure.

ASEAN cannot make decisions members regard as vital because its Charter makes consultation and consensus the basic rule. Military access and diplomatic positions remain national calls; regional cooperation can extend only over common rules and supplier choices but cannot remove conflict between foreign laws. It also cannot guarantee that members give identical answers, since Singapore and the Philippines joined Washington's Pax Silica initiative while others backed China's World AI Cooperation Organisation.

ASEAN further cannot make other members bear the cost of a decision one member takes for itself. When China held up imports of Philippine bananas during the 2012 stand-off at Scarborough Shoal, no other member was obliged to compensate the Philippines. Its looseness is what has kept all but one founding member in place over almost 60 years and prevented either great power from shutting out another.

Ng Chee Khern proposes three ways to make ASEAN more dependable: keeping geography from dividing it by treating Mekong water security as a regional concern, making uneven integration acceptable through compensation that the European Union provides but ASEAN lacks, and building public support across generations so younger people have a stake in its future. As chair he would consult early when members face pressure, help set deadlines for permits after an undersea cable broke in April 2024, agree on electricity export rules with Thailand, and develop common standards applied credibly by every member.

In the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute's 2026 survey ASEAN was first named as the party regional opinion leaders had most confidence in to uphold the rules-based order, narrowly ahead of America at 23.4 per cent against 22.3 per cent. Yet the same survey shows slowness and ineffectiveness remain the commonest concern, a tension Ng Chee Khern says reflects the price of never being outvoted on vital matters rather than any failure to honour commitments.
items.title: ASEAN Can Improve Singapore's Strategic Choices But Cannot Replace Its Own Capabilities

OpenAI fixed a bug that had wrongly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage, but the correction means those models now consume allowances 40% faster on comparable tasks.

Tibo Sottiaux of OpenAI said the same work will use more of users' plan allowance after the fix, reaching limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol compared with last week.

OpenAI says both models still outperform their predecessors—GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol—in usage efficiency despite the change.

The company will not charge users for the extra consumption from the billing error, but it is offering one banked usage reset to Go, Plus, Pro, and Business subscribers that expires a month later.

Indian equities climbed to multi-month closing highs, with the Sensex and Nifty advancing on easing tariff concerns. The gains came despite a US proposal of 25% tariffs on India announced November 25.

The BSE Sensex rose 0.5% to close at 84,328.6, its strongest level since January 7. The NSE Nifty 50 advanced 0.3% to 25,884.5, reaching its highest closing point since February 11.

Both indices sit roughly 1% away from wiping out their losses for the year. Foreign inflows of about $15 billion this month added further support and placed India among the best-performing major global equity markets.

Sunny Agrawal of SBI Capital Markets said tariff worries were concentrated in home textile, shrimp, and high US-exposure businesses, while pharmaceuticals and semiconductors appeared unlikely to be hit. He expects frontline indices to move into consolidation with sector rotation over the next two months, possibly extending until the Union Budget.
items.title: Sensex and Nifty Reach Multi-Month Highs as Tariff Fears Ease

Over the past eight trading sessions, India's blue-chip indices rose while smaller stocks fell, signaling a narrowing rally concentrated in large caps. The Sensex and Nifty each gained more than 2% over that period.

The gains came at the expense of lower-priced segments: the BSE 150 Midcap index dropped 1.2%, the BSE 250 Smallcap index fell 1.9%, and the BSE 250 Microcap index lost 4.2% over the same eight sessions.

Market breadth deteriorated across most segments, with six of the last eight sessions showing weakness in both the Nifty Smallcap 250 and Nifty Microcap 250 indices, four weak sessions in the Nifty Midcap 150, seven in the BSE 1000 index.

In the B Group of roughly 1,900 smaller mainboard stocks, an average of three out of every five stocks declined over the period, down from two out of every three advancing earlier in November. The MT Group's about 70 SME companies also saw weakening breadth across six sessions, while the X Group's around 1,100 micro-cap stocks posted seven consecutive sessions of negative breadth.

Analysts attributed the divergence to foreign investor buying concentrated in large caps through index funds and exchange-traded funds. Media, metals, PSU banks and SME stocks were among the weakest performers over the past week.
items.title: Large-cap-led rally narrows as market breadth weakens across mid- and small-caps

Avarta Capital is raising a ₹7,500 crore ($1 billion) private equity fund that would become the largest homegrown Indian PE fund if it reaches its target. Amal Parikh will take over as managing partner of the firm and make a significant investment in the new vehicle.

The onshore fund has already collected soft commitments from domestic family offices and received regulatory approval in August, with sources expecting a final close by end of March.

Puneet Bhatia, an anchor investor in Avarta's debut fund, will mentor the new capital while retaining his role as partner and executive chairman at TPG Capital Asia. He continues to serve India operations for that firm.

Parikh said narrowing opportunities in Indian listed markets have pushed him toward private investments, projecting annualised returns of 20-25% could benefit both managers and investors.

items.summary:
Faisal Islam argues that the tariff announcement this week is a weaker and more tentative move than last April, with no dramatic rhetoric or immediate implementation.

The rates are upper ceilings set to take effect only in January or February after consultation, following eight months of hearings. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said negotiators expect broad talks about industrial overcapacity before finalizing the measures.

Analysts worldwide see this as an effort to shore up domestic legal footing rather than a fundamental shift in Trump's trade agenda. The forced-labour basis is being replaced partly by claims that allies harm US goods exports, though the UK remains caught at 10% extra on global tariffs and was unaffected.

With the Supreme Court having struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year, two legal bases now underpin the tariffs for many countries. A group of 25 states has sued to strike down the forced-labour tariffs, while Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries says the new House will move aggressively in its first 100 days to repeal them.

The China rate of 20% matches last year's truce, which is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing responded with no retaliation and dismissed overcapacity as a false issue. US share of Chinese exports has fallen to around 10% this year from 15% two years ago and 19% in 2018.

Canada tariffs are the most politically exposed, since more than half rely on Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley act. A Senate bill already seeks repeal, with possible Republican support to override a veto, while interim deals appear acceptable to senators such as Chris Coons.
items.title: Analyst says Trump's new tariffs pose less threat than April

New Zealand's governing National-led coalition won 40 seats in the 130-seat parliament but fell one vote short of an outright majority, meaning it must secure support from the centrist Opportunity Party to stay in power. If no agreement is reached with that party—which holds seven seats and has been called this election's kingmaker—the country may return to the polls.

The National Party under Prime Minister Christopher Luxon took 40 seats, while its coalition partners ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First won 13 and 12 respectively. The centre-left Labour Party secured 36 seats, with The Greens taking 17 and Te Pāti Māori five. A Labour-led government was not possible even if Opportunity backed it.

The official Friday tally showed the National bloc had lost two seats on special votes compared with preliminary results from election day on November 7. Those overseas or absent-voter ballots typically skew toward left-leaning parties, which narrowed what had looked like a slim lead for the right.

Voters campaigned amid concerns about living costs and unemployment. Labour pledged to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel prices and expand social housing support, while National focused on lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation and greater defence spending. Many voters expressed apathy toward their leaders in earlier interviews with the BBC.

A survey by the Helen Clark Foundation found that more than half of New Zealanders no longer see the country as a land of opportunity. Record numbers of residents have emigrated to Australia, including former Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.

Taiwanese voters cast ballots on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the ruling Democratic Progressive Party as it navigates a precarious position amid intense pressure from Beijing.

The vote across 22 districts mostly pits DPP candidates against opposition Kuomintang challengers and focuses on bread-and-butter issues like housing affordability, though China's military posture and alleged interference cast a large shadow over an election usually dominated by local concerns.

Taiwanese officials reported thousands of suspected misinformation incidents and hundreds of AI-generated videos targeting politicians disliked by Beijing, while China dismissed the claims as fabricated attempts to stoke anti-China sentiment; its Taiwan affairs office spokesperson Zhu Fenglian said such allegations 'stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes'.

The mayoral race for Taipei is especially contentious because it pits a DPP candidate against an incumbent KMT leader who has held the post for three decades, and Beijing declared the DPP's challenger Puma Shen a 'diehard separatist' in 2024.

Political scientist Wei-Ting Yen of Academia Sinica said even though local elections are not about China, their outcome will have huge implications for cross-strait relations, while noting that if the KMT loses traditional strongholds Beijing may reconsider its influence strategy.

President Lai Ching-te has adopted a harder line on Taiwan than his predecessor Tsai Ing-wen and proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending to reach above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for next year, but many voters want the money spent on economic issues instead of weapons.

Taiwan's economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year—the fastest rate in 50 years—largely driven by its semiconductor industry, yet nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) over the same period.

Analysts say DPP and KMT national leaders have stayed out of most mayoral races because campaigns are focused on local issues, though Lai hopes to use momentum from strong challengers in the upcoming 2028 presidential elections.
items.title: China's shadow looms over Taiwan's local elections

items.summary:
Ali Kololo, a Kenyan woodcutter wrongly sentenced to death over the 2011 attack and abduction of British couple David and Judith Tebbutt, told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police destroyed his life. Somali gunmen killed David on their beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011 and held Judith captive in Somalia for six months.

Met detectives led by former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd arrived to support the investigation within days of the attack, even though the UK government had instructed them not to accept information obtained from interrogating detainees. Kololo is suing the Met over his conviction, which he says was secured through misleading evidence and unlawful conduct.

Hibberd relied on a statement that Kenyan police forced Kololo to sign under torture while he was illiterate, claiming it linked him to the attack even though the arresting officer said Kololo had been barefoot. Hibberd also told the court that Kololo wore shoes matching footwear marks found at the resort, without disclosing that Met forensic examination could not establish whether those shoes made the marks.

Kololo faced trial without a lawyer and cross-examined witnesses himself through an interpreter speaking Swahili, which was not his first language. He said he believed he was framed because he was poor and lacked resources to defend himself. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

The UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct found that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial and would have faced gross misconduct proceedings, but could not be disciplined after retiring from the force. At the time, a lawyer said Hibberd disagreed with the report's findings.

Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction in April 2023 over doubts about the prosecution's evidence, following years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and Kenyan lawyer Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free. Judith Tebbutt had also believed he was innocent and said she thought he had been scapegoated.

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he still suffers from torture and prison trauma, is too frail to work as a woodcutter, lives alone in a mud hut, and struggles to feed himself amid erratic rain. His wife divorced him while he was imprisoned, their children went to live with his mother, dropped out of school over fees, and barely remember him.

The Met has not apologised or admitted wrongdoing and is contesting Kololo's compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve. The force said it did not wish to comment on the claim but expressed support for those affected by the crime.

Preetha Gopalan of Reprieve described the Met's conduct in the case as 'egregious' and accused them of spending 10 years evading accountability while dragging Kololo through court, leaving his ordeal unresolved.
items.title: Kenyan Man Wrongly Sentenced Over Attack on UK Couple Says Met Police Ruined His Life

The growth rate quickened from 15.5 percent in the January-September period, per figures from the National Bureau of Statistics.

A widely reported shortage of elevator and escalator mechanics is worsening in the US and other countries, leaving building managers sometimes waiting days for repairs to begin.

In the US the average salary for an elevator mechanic reaches $110,000 (£83,000), yet recruiters say it remains hard to attract new workers into a trade that requires years of training.

The National Association for Elevator Contractors points to a four-year apprenticeship and state licensing as early barriers, while weeks- or months-long repair delays are usually blamed on unavailable parts rather than staff shortages; manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder can take six to 12 weeks.

A UK consultant says the shortage is also bad and worsening there, with food delivery firms reportedly refusing flats whose lifts are out of service, and suggests tax breaks for training companies could help draw in new workers.

The Lift and Escalator Industry Association notes that reaching competency takes time and calls continued investment essential, reporting 259 active lift and escalator apprentices currently in the UK.
items.title: US and UK face a growing shortage of elevator mechanics

items.summary:
Oil prices rebounded from their recent slump as renewed Middle East supply threats outweighed earlier surplus concerns, with Brent crude for January delivery rising 1.3% to $95.90 per barrel and WTI climbing 1.2% to $84.65 per barrel on Thursday.

Yemen's Houthi forces claimed strikes that set fires at Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, with satellite imagery showing thick black smoke over the site, while separate attacks near Riyadh's financial district injured 11 people after a strike hit a tower housing the Public Investment Fund for the second time in under a week.

U.S. commercial crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, marking a third consecutive weekly build as higher net imports and domestic output outweighed increased refinery runs while exports fell to their lowest level since early August.

Standard Chartered analysts say oil is unlikely to sink below recent lows without clearer evidence of sustained inventory builds or faster recovery in physical supply, arguing the price correction has already discounted much of the anticipated surplus that the IEA reinforced with a 3.3mb/d upward revision to its Q4 supply estimate reflecting quicker Gulf production and export recovery.

The analysts point to broad easing across refined product prices, refining margins, and freight rates as evidence that geopolitical tightness is unwinding, noting European jet fuel declined 24% month-to-date while Asian fuel oil fell 31%, the European diesel crack dropped 21%, Asian FCC and NWE hydrocracking margins each slid 25%, Middle East-to-China clean product freight rates fell 27%, and dirty VLCC Gulf-to-China freight rates plunged 55%.

The easing occurs against uncertain Washington-Tehran diplomacy, with StanChart saying a diplomatic breakthrough could accelerate physical flows and reinforce downward pressure while renewed disruptions to export infrastructure or shipping routes could quickly challenge surplus expectations.
items.title: Standard Chartered Says Oil Needs a New Shock to Fall Further

items.summary:
The UK government has cancelled two long-awaited major road projects in the East Midlands, diverting more than £400m into defence spending. Upgrades to roundabouts on the A38 around Derby and improvements to the Newark bypass on the A46 have been shelved.

A Treasury review in June requested departmental funding cuts to shore up the UK's defence budget, with the Department for Transport told to cut capital spending. The DfT said it axed the two schemes after input from National Highways to prioritise investment in national defence now and for the future.

The cancellations reduce planned road spending by £428m over the next four years. The two projects' estimated budgets to completion would have been more than £1bn combined, though the DfT indicated it would keep them on the table.

Regional mayor Claire Ward criticised the decision as disappointing and short-sighted, arguing that weakening East Midlands infrastructure undermines the region's ability to grow its economy. Environmental campaigners welcomed the move, with Transport Action Network calling it an opportunity for local decision makers to find cheaper solutions.
items.title: UK government cancels two East Midlands road schemes to fund defence

Nvidia has frozen chip orders for buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia as Washington restricts China's access to American compute. The pause targets countries that have granted Chinese hyperscalers legal entry to export-controlled Nvidia chips.

The holdup risks Nvidia's business in the region—its Singapore arm booked $104 billion in 2025—as well as AI expansion in one of the world's fastest-growing data center markets.

The move comes amid scrutiny over an affair between the Nvidia CEO and a Singapore-based executive, alongside broader US efforts to curb chip exports and smuggling. The Wall Street Journal characterized these actions as putting America 'in the driver's seat of the most consequential technological race of the superpower rivalry.'
items.title: Nvidia Halts Chip Shipments to Southeast Asia

items.summary:
Piramal Pharma raised its full-year earnings outlook for fiscal year 2027 after reporting strong third-quarter results, with analysts projecting a 15-23% upside to the company's estimates.

CDMO revenue jumped 36% year-on-year to Rs 1,424 crore in the September quarter, driven by stronger demand, improved execution and higher capacity utilisation. Innovation-related work accounted for 49% of CDMO revenue in the first half of FY27 versus 46% a year earlier, while differentiated offerings rose to 43% from 40%.

The company expects strong growth in high-value businesses such as on-patent manufacturing and antibody-drug conjugates (ADC) to support margins in coming quarters. Complex Hospital Generics delivered 32% revenue growth in the quarter, led by ex-US inhalation anaesthesia sales and the ramp-up of the recently acquired Kenalog injectable portfolio.

The consumer healthcare division grew 13% in the quarter on strength from power brands and e-commerce. Piramal noted that expiry of the low-margin Bayer distribution agreement may weigh on revenue but could improve consolidated Ebitda margin by around 50 basis points.

Motilal Oswal Financial Services raised its FY27-FY28 earnings estimates by 7-11%, citing an improved CDMO demand outlook, scaling of the ADC business and stronger supplier collaboration. ICICI Securities lifted its Ebitda estimates for the period by 1-6%, supported by strong customer enquiries, new molecule additions and a growing commercial pipeline.
items.title: Piramal Pharma raises FY27 growth guidance as CDMO revenue surges

A five-day wedding in Bihar for the younger daughter of Mokama MLA Anant Singh has drawn worldwide media coverage, with outlets highlighting its ostentatious scale against a backdrop where one in three citizens is multidimensionally poor.

The BBC described the event as 'a royal wedding' and reported that a political rival called for a probe into how the money was spent. The Guardian headlined that the politician hosted 400,000 guests at his daughter's wedding in India's poorest state, noting six helipads were built for it.

The event took place on Nov 25 when Shivangi married Rishikesh Kumar alias Ankit. Invitations extended across India and into Pakistan, with the MLA saying anyone who attended would be a gift to him.

Preparations included more than 10 bighas (6.2 acres) developed into a venue featuring a Jaipur-inspired pavilion, a massive stage and imported flowers. The groom's procession comprised 151 vehicles, while the bride's 'bidaai' was scheduled for Thursday.

Food arrangements struggled despite 500 cooks and over 300 cooking stations serving more than 150 dishes on the menu. Videos showed guests scrambling to catch disposable plates thrown into crowds, with some using cardboard or drinking glasses to carry food.

A horse race featuring over 20 horses from Bihar, UP, Rajasthan and Delhi offered a Thar to the winner but had its finale postponed after spectators climbed trees and high-tension towers. Traffic stretched for 8-10 km, stranding commuters and VIPs including assembly speaker Prem Kumar's convoy.

Animal welfare activist Naresh Kadyan of the Animal Welfare Board of India has submitted a legal notice over alleged coercive handling of an elephant with an iron 'ankush' and sought an independent inquiry into the horse-racing event.
items.title: Bihar MLA's lavish daughter wedding draws global media attention amid criminal cases

items.summary:
Union home minister Amit Shah said on Thursday that India is playing a leading role in the global fight against terrorism, according to reports.

Shah attributed this leadership to his government's 'zero tolerance' policy toward terror and its decisive action against every form of terrorism and terror conspiracy.

He made the remarks while paying homage to victims of the 26/11 attacks that struck Mumbai 18 years ago, saluting soldiers who died in responding to terrorists and innocent people killed by them.

Shah said his government's zero tolerance approach against terrorism is being praised worldwide.
items.title: Amit Shah Says India Leads Global Fight Against Terrorism

WhatsApp has launched scheduled messaging, allowing users to write a message now and set it to be sent anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later.

The feature is available for both one-on-one conversations and group chats. Users can schedule text messages as well as photos and videos.

To use the function, users type their message and press and hold the send button, which opens a menu where they select the desired date and time. Scheduled messages appear to recipients like regular ones.

WhatsApp says scheduled messages will be sent at the chosen time even if the sender's phone is off or has run out of battery. Users can also view all scheduled messages and delete them before sending.

The company said in a blog post that scheduled messages remain end-to-end encrypted, so no one else—not WhatsApp—can read them. The feature is rolling out globally over the coming weeks.
items.title: WhatsApp Adds Scheduled Messaging Feature

The proposed measures reflect growing concern that Chinese goods may reach the US market through third countries. The US Trade Representative reportedly referred to China more than 250 times in its assessment of Vietnam and more than 300 times in its assessment of the European Union, signaling focus beyond direct bilateral relations with Beijing.

Trump's administration has also proposed increasing tariffs on China by 20 percentage points above the existing duties. This would raise the total tariff burden to 45% if implemented as described, though the increase remains subject to the current US-China trade understanding.

The strategy offered countries like India a chance to attract investment and integrate into global supply chains while retaining Chinese operations. Washington's expanding trade policy now complicates this equation by pressuring nations that maintain strong economic links with Beijing.

Trump's second-term tariff agenda follows the Supreme Court striking down his April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariffs, which had escalated duties on several trading partners before China emerged as a significant challenger to Washington's approach. The current proposals leave room for renewed escalation as the existing trade arrangement approaches its January expiry.

Capital Economics' chief Asia economist Mark Williams told Reuters that the latest measures could give Washington additional leverage if trade tensions resume with Beijing.

Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani said Wednesday that he feels regret about the 2026 season, during which a left knee injury ended his pitching and the team missed its third consecutive World Series title. The 32-year-old last pitched on July 3 before his batting also declined toward the end of the year.

Ohtani told an online interview that it is hard to attribute his injuries to one single factor. He said he and the Dodgers have various plans for how he should handle his two-way role next season, with both sides sharing the view that Ohtani needs to be in good condition heading into October's postseason.

The team has indicated a possibility of delaying Ohtani's return to pitching. Ohtani noted it is not ideal for a pitcher to make too few appearances but that pitching too often would also carry risk, and he said there are several ways to manage this, whether by pushing himself harder or spacing out his appearances over the season.

Ohtani addressed a possible lockout if Major League Baseball and the players' union fail to reach a new collective bargaining agreement after the current one expires next month. He warned that any wasted period could build fatigue from unnecessary pitching practice, calling it a tricky point. Despite this uncertainty, he reaffirmed his commitment to remaining a two-way player because the role lets him contribute most while using his strengths.

Looking ahead to what would be Ohtani's 10th MLB season, he said he wants to make the best of the offseason and use next year to overcome the frustrations of the current one.
items.title: Ohtani Expresses Regret After Injury-Plagued Dodgers Season

items.summary:
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating a near-miss in which a Qantas plane aborted its landing at Sydney airport after spotting an Air New Zealand aircraft crossing the runway during descent.

Qantas flight 426 from Melbourne was due to land just before 10.15am on Wednesday, and had been told to expect late clearance because of aircraft crossing the runway.

The crew saw the other plane while still approaching and elected a go-around rather than landing without clearance.

The ATSB said it would examine what information each crew received and what 'mental models' they held during the incident, noting that safety defences such as the go-around decision were in place.

A preliminary report is expected within about eight weeks.
items.title: ATSB investigating close call between Qantas and Air New Zealand planes at Sydney airport

items.summary:
Altria Group and Japan Tobacco are exploring a potential takeover of British cigarette maker Imperial Brands in what could become one of the largest U.K. acquisitions in a decade.

Richmond, Virginia-based Altria said Thursday it is considering a possible bid for Imperial with a third party.

This follows earlier reports that Japan Tobacco was weighing partnering on an Imperial deal and splitting up its assets across different parts of the world.

A completed transaction would add Imperial to a wave of high-profile companies leaving London's stock exchange as foreign buyers and private capital take advantage of lower valuations in the U.K. equity market, which is struggling to attract new listings.
items.title: Altria, Japan Tobacco Explore Takeover of Imperial Brands

items.summary:
Better Victoria and FixVictoria, two unofficial Victorian election lobby groups with undisclosed funding, spent up to $355,000 and $262,000 respectively on social media ads ahead of the state election. Combined, their ad spending exceeded that of the official Victorian Labor account between August 26 and November 26.

The two groups' ads have been viewed more than 39 million times across Facebook, Instagram and Google's network, ABC NEWS Verify reports. FixVictoria's ads focus on government debt depicted as a flood 'tsunami', while Better Victoria targets potholes and infrastructure projects; both appear sympathetic to the Liberal Party position.

A Victorian election law loophole means advertisers promoting issues rather than specific candidates or parties are not required to disclose their funding, so neither group revealed who is behind them. Meta did not respond to questions about transparency around the ads' financing.

FixVictoria's public face Gideon Rozner said it is a private membership organisation of roughly 30-60 unidentified individuals and insisted it was non-partisan; its budget runs closer to $2 million, according to an insider. Election marketer Toby Ralph has run more than 50 campaigns globally and made the group's ads while also insisting they avoid contact with politicians.

Better Victoria lists lawyer Ron Holzer as secretary but says funding comes entirely from members through advertising agency Bench Media; it kept running ads into the official election period, which its spokesperson said was legal.
items.title: Two hidden lobby groups spent hundreds of thousands on Victoria's election ads

items.summary:
SpiceJet keeps flying by settling debts with creditors instead of facing insolvency, even as its fleet shrinks and regulators question whether it can safely operate. The airline's survival rests on repeated debt-to-equity deals rather than a genuine turnaround.

India expects passenger traffic to grow sixfold to around 1.1 billion by 2040 (ev1), which would open room for more airlines, yet SpiceJet is moving in the opposite direction. Its domestic market share peaked at about 21% in July 2014 (ev3) and fell to just 0.6% by September 2026 (ev6).

The decline shows up sharply in passenger numbers: SpiceJet carried roughly 73,000 domestic passengers in September 2026 (ev7), down from nearly 5.9 lakh in January of that year (ev8). The Boeing 737 Max grounding once affected about a fifth of its fleet (ev9).

A brief accounting reprieve made the turnaround look possible: SpiceJet reported a standalone net profit of ₹58 crore for FY25 (ev10), and its net worth turned positive at ₹683 crore as of March 31, 2025 (ev11). But it still recorded an operating loss of around ₹470 crore in FY25 (ev13), auditors kept flagging material uncertainty about going concern, and accumulated losses remained substantial.

The airline funds operations through fresh capital raises. In September 2024 it raised a ₹3,000 crore QIP (ev15) that was meant to restore operations but had already used around ₹2,699 crore by March 2025 (ev17). It also reallocated ₹300 crore originally earmarked for new fleet induction—shifting ₹150 crore to general corporate purposes and another ₹150 crore to settle creditors (ev18, ev20).

Its creditors include aircraft lessors such as Carlyle Aviation, Aircastle and Genesis, airport operators, ground handlers, suppliers and banks. Between April and September 2026 it owed small businesses ₹123 crore, of which ₹63 crore remained unpaid for more than 45 days (ev21, ev22). Carlyle agreed to restructure around $90 million in lease arrears through write-offs, convertible debentures and equity.

This creates a vicious cycle: without enough aircraft it cannot earn the revenue needed to pay suppliers, lessors and employees on time, so providers hesitate to extend credit and more planes stay grounded. Last week its board approved raising up to ₹5,500 crore through instruments that could include equity shares, debt and convertible instruments (ev24), along with increasing authorised share capital from ₹2,000 crore to ₹7,500 crore.

Creditors keep agreeing to settlements because a negotiated deal may recover more than the little they might get after a long insolvency process. Under India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, recovery depends on where each claim sits in the payment waterfall—secured creditors rank above employee dues and unsecured financial creditors—and aircraft lessors can hold repossession rights that ordinary suppliers lack.

The proposed fundraise could enable more debt-to-equity conversions with creditors, but equityholders are paid last. The turnaround ultimately hinges on getting planes back into service and running flights reliably. Without another round of funding the airline may collapse.
items.title: SpiceJet survives on settlements and funding rounds despite collapsing operations

items.summary:
Australian police have recovered part of a stolen Melbourne Cup trophy, along with approximately 2 kilograms of melted gold seized from a property in Elsternwick. The top portion of the 2003 Melbourne Cup was among the items taken by detectives.

Police allege four Melbourne Cups were stolen from Flemington Racecourse on November 16 this month. Separately, investigators located what is believed to be the melted-down 1948 Caulfield Cup in the Melbourne area after it was allegedly sold to a third party following its theft from Caulfield on November 4.

A 39-year-old man from Elsternwick was arrested over the Caulfield theft and charged with two counts each of burglary and theft, plus possessing a drug of dependence. He was re-arrested the next day in relation to the Flemington theft, facing charges including burglary, theft, handling stolen goods, and dealing property suspected of being proceeds of crime.

The Elsternwick man has been bailed to appear before Moorabbin Magistrates' Court on March 1. Earlier this month, a 36-year-old man from Mount Waverley was arrested over the alleged Melbourne Cup thefts and charged with burglary, theft, committing an indictable offence whilst on bail, and dealing property suspected of being proceeds of crime.

That second suspect is scheduled to appear before Melbourne Magistrates' Court on February 23.
items.title: Detectives Recover Part of Stolen Melbourne Cup

items.summary:
Scroll found that Uttar Pradesh's biggest voter deletions during its Special Intensive Revision fell on constituencies where the BJP won, with 20 of the 25 seats showing the highest deletions being BJP strongholds. The analysis compared draft assembly-level electoral rolls released in November against those used in the 2024 Lok Sabha election.

Chief Minister Adityanath said at a December 2025 party meeting that about four crore voters were missing and that roughly 90% of them were BJP supporters rather than opponents. The Election Commission's revision between November 2025 and April 2026 removed more than two crore voters, or about 13.4%, from the rolls.

The state then added nearly 19 lakh new voters through Form 6 enrolment before beginning a separate special summary revision on November 17 to update lists and register younger voters turning 18 by January 1 of the following year.

Allahabad North had the largest net deletion in percentage terms at 34.4%, followed closely by Lucknow Cantt, seat of deputy chief minister Brijesh Pathak, at 34.3%. These are mostly urban constituencies where the BJP has consistently won over three decades.
items.title: BJP's UP strongholds saw the largest voter deletions in a special electoral roll revision

visual.alt: Bar chart. BJP-led seats 12.9 %; Samajwadi Party-led seats 10.7 %.

items.summary:
The Allahabad High Court has said the legislature may consider reducing India's age of juvenility from 18 years to 16, following a Kerala High Court verdict. Justice Abdul Shahid made the remark while dismissing a juvenile's appeal against rejection of his second bail application in a dacoity-murder case.

In its judgment, the Kerala High Court observed that it is high time for legislatures to amend statutes dealing with juveniles and children in conflict with law to reduce the age to 16 years. The court pointed to present trends showing sufficient maturity among children when they reach 16.

Justice Shahid's order dated November 17 noted these Kerala High Court observations on the maturity attained by children at 16, adding that this aspect may be duly considered by the legislature.
items.title: Allahabad HC says legislature may lower juvenility age to 16

items.summary:
An EU summit convened to break a deadlock over the bloc's next seven-year budget ended in disorder after leaders refused to abandon their positions and openly doubted whether a deal could be reached by December.

European Council President Antonio Costa pressed members toward his compromise proposal worth about €1.78 trillion across seven years, roughly 10% below the original draft, but it drew fierce rejection from both sides of the divide.

The talks split into two camps: seven 'Frugals' pushing for deeper cuts and 17 'Friends of Cohesion' resisting them, with Costa's plan seen as overly favorable to France.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told reporters a deal was 'light years away,' while Dutch leader Rob Jetten dismissed any deadline. French President Emmanuel Macron issued an ultimatum that negotiations would not reopen after December 31 and called Costa's cuts a strategic mistake, though other states viewed the threat as a tactic to extract concessions.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz took a hardline frugal stance, vowing cuts beyond the €204 billion in Costa's plan. The deep Paris-Berlin divide cast doubt over progress, with Merz saying talks were moving 'yes and no.'

The Frugals boycotted Costa's small-group format after feeling unfairly targeted, while Macron's mid-summit press conference wiped out hopes of a breakthrough.

Costa said the goal remains delivering a new budget from January 1, 2028, to avoid spilling into the 2027 electoral cycle. A diplomat described the proceedings as 'political theatre,' noting there were no detailed negotiations.
items.title: EU budget summit ends in disarray as leaders hold firm on red lines

items.summary:
Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar questioned the decision to leave out Ravindra Jadeja from India's playing XI for the second Test against New Zealand in Christchurch, arguing that his bowling could have been useful on a pitch expected to offer little assistance to spinners. Gavaskar noted that Jadeja is India's third-highest wicket-taker in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle and said he believed the left-arm spinner would have made an impact on the fourth and fifth days of the match.

Gavaskar pointed out that while public discussion has focused mainly on pacer Mohammed Siraj, who was also omitted from the XI, Jadeja's exclusion deserved equal attention. He described Jadeja as someone known to grip and turn the ball on placid pitches and said his spin would have been valuable later in the Test.

Despite raising questions about Jadeja's omission, Gavaskar backed the team selected by management. He emphasized that once a playing XI is announced, supporters should stand behind it regardless of reservations over the final 11, 14, or 16 players and expressed hope for a strong performance from India.

India captain Shubman Gill won the toss before play at Hagley Oval in Christchurch and elected to bowl first. The side made one change to its lineup by handing Test debutant pacer Gurnoor Brar his first appearance after Prasidh Krishna was dropped following the drawn first Test in Wellington. New Zealand fielded the same playing XI for what is being treated as a series-deciding match.

India's playing XI includes KL Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal, Shubman Gill (captain), Rishabh Pant (wicketkeeper), Washington Sundar, Dhruv Jurel, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar, and Jasprit Bumrah. New Zealand's lineup features Tom Latham as captain with Devon Conway, Henry Nicholls, Rachin Ravindra, Daryl Mitchell, Tom Blundell (wicketkeeper), Glenn Phillips, Nathan Smith, Kyle Jamieson, Matt Henry, and Jacob Duffy.
items.title: Gavaskar Questions Jadeja's Omission as India Field Test XI Against New Zealand

items.summary:
Police arrested a 21-year-old man on Thursday for murdering his 25-year-old business partner over a financial dispute and burying the body near an abandoned water tank in Sector 63A of Gurugram.

The accused, identified as Bablu from Badaun district in Uttar Pradesh, was taken into custody after four days of police custody. He was arrested at his native village on Friday.

Police allege that Bablu stabbed the victim and strangled him with a cotton scarf before burying the body and covering it with soil. They also reportedly burnt their clothes to destroy evidence.

The victim, Naim, who sold peanuts in partnership with Bablu for four to five years, went missing on November 8 after an altercation over financial transactions. His brother filed a complaint at Sector 65 police station on November 11.
items.title: Man Arrested for Killing Business Partner and Burying Body Near Water Tank in Gurugram

items.summary:
The Centre's flagship PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is nearing installations in about seven million households, having released nearly ₹38,000 crore in subsidies nationwide. Officials say the program remains on track toward its target of covering ten million households by March 27, 2027.

According to Ministry of New and Renewable Energy data as of November 26, about 6.91 million households have benefited from the scheme, with ₹37,989 crore released in subsidies and a total installed rooftop capacity of 20.2 GW across the country.

The program was launched in February 2024 and offers subsidies up to ₹78,000 per household for installing a 3KW solar panel system. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit on November 2 that the scheme now covers nearly one lakh new homes every six days and has cut electricity bills by roughly 76%.

A QR-code tool launched in August to simplify installations has logged about 4,50,000 scans over three months. Of those users, around 98,110 generated customized solar plans while 46,369 used the click-to-call feature to contact certified local vendors.

In the week between November 16 and November 23 alone, the portal recorded about 47,000 fresh scans, producing roughly 8,442 new solar plans and 4,159 direct vendor calls in seven days.
items.title: India's PM solar rooftop scheme nears seven million household installations

items.summary:
In several West Bengal districts, police began visiting voters whose names were deleted or put under adjudication during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and asking them to submit identity and family documents. The visits have triggered fresh anxiety over citizenship even among people who already submitted papers to election tribunals.

The drive started on Tuesday (November 24) without public notice, according to a booth-level officer quoted by The Federal. It has been conducted in districts including Malda, Jalpaiguri, South Dinajpur, East Burdwan, Bankura, South 24 Parganas, Hooghly, Howrah, and the East and West Midnapore areas.

Officers are collecting names, Electors Photo Identity Card numbers, assembly constituencies, police station jurisdictions, birth certificates, school records, parents' educational documents, land papers, and details of whether voters or their parents appeared in the 2002 electoral rolls. In Jalpaiguri a camp was set up at Dhupguri to check deleted voters' documents.

The chief electoral officer's office said it had neither issued instructions for the exercise nor been informed about it, and some district election officials reported receiving no formal communication. Booth-level officers also learned of the visits only after residents called them for clarification.

Some police officers confirmed they received orders from state police to carry out the drive, with sources saying those instructions came from state police headquarters. A senior Howrah officer said the exercise aims to speed up disposal of appeals in view of Supreme Court efforts to expedite SIR-related cases; on November 23 the apex court directed the election commission to increase appellate tribunals and prioritize deleted-voter appeals.

In Unsani village, Howrah residents questioned police authority when officers could not produce written instructions or receipts for collected documents. The drive coincided with an election commission directive asking booth-level officers to check voter details such as names, parents' names, dates of birth, addresses, and photographs.

There is no official indication that the visits are meant to establish citizenship or target suspected undocumented migrants, and the government has not clarified how collected information will be used. Trinamool Congress MP Samirul Islam said police should not take on a role belonging to election officials, while CPI(M) secretary Mohammed Salim questioned re-examining papers already submitted to tribunals.

BJP state president Shamik Bhattacharya defended the action as internal-security work under the rule of law. Separately, the state government added electoral roll status to eligibility for its Bharosa unemployment assistance scheme and set a target of issuing three lakh Citizenship Amendment Act certificates by December 31.
items.title: Police document drives for deleted Bengal voters raise citizenship concerns

items.summary:
Community-based forest concessions in the Democratic Republic of Congo are expanding rapidly, yet experts warn that legal titles alone do not guarantee conservation or income for local communities. The initiative is awarding land rights to roughly 7.1 million hectares (about 17.5 million acres), an area comparable to Ireland.

The number of community forest concessions has grown from eight in 2017 to more than 350 by 2026, with at least 236 legally established. Titles provide communities protection against arbitrary expropriation and a sense of security, but they must also create economic opportunities or some residents resort to illegal exploitation.

Experts Blaise Mudodosi and Védaste Cituli identify weak coordination between government agencies as a central obstacle, noting that permits should be issued free yet communities are sometimes forced to pay officials. They point to limited technical capacity, poor market access in remote areas lacking roads and electricity, underdeveloped local entrepreneurship, and insufficient NGO support for developing management plans.

Only 67 of the concessions have basic management plans identifying resources and use rules; logging continues where such plans are missing or poorly understood by communities. Some residents report that promised carbon markets never materialized, leaving them to exploit forests as before.
items.title: DRC community forestry expands but faces profitability and governance hurdles

items.summary:
Ahead of Sunday's Spanish snap election, social media is circulating claims that the vote could be rigged to favor outgoing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist government. These allegations misrepresent how Spain's electoral system actually works.

The most widespread claim concerns immigration. A widely shared post alleges that residents of Alcorcón near Madrid discovered strangers had been fraudulently registered at their addresses, allegedly undocumented Moroccan migrants. The source article comes from La Gaceta, a media outlet owned by a foundation chaired by far-right Vox leader Santiago Abascal.

Alcorcón's municipal authorities denied allegations of mass fraudulent registrations and said the two specific cases cited in the article had already been resolved. More fundamentally, being listed on Spain's padrón municipal does not grant voting rights; Spanish nationality is required to vote in parliamentary elections. So even a fraudulently registered undocumented migrant could not legally cast a ballot.

Spain's postal voting system has also drawn suspicion as a possible tool for manipulating results, with Abascal urging voters against using it. Experts told AFP that safeguards exist: applicants must verify their identity twice, once when applying and again when submitting the envelope, which is securely stored by the postal service until election day.

Other online allegations target Indra, a Spanish technology company partly owned by the state involved in elections. Users suggest Sánchez could exploit his stake to manipulate vote counts. But Indra does not count ballots; votes are counted manually at polling stations in public view and can be observed by party representatives. Indra only processes and communicates preliminary results on election night, with official figures later verified by electoral authorities.

While none of these viral claims provides evidence of a rigged election, their circulation is fueling distrust in Spain's electoral process before the polls open.
items.title: Spain Debunks Viral Claims That Its Snap Election Is Being Rigged

items.summary:
Three party leaders are competing in Spain's general election on Sunday, which leftist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called after a parliamentary defeat over housing legislation exposed the fragility of his minority coalition government.

Javier Carbonell, policy analyst at the European Policy Centre speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, said that despite solid economic growth, citizens remain angry about the housing crisis and inflation. He argued voters are frustrated with both the government and the broader economic system regardless of positive macroeconomic data.

Carbonell added that while anger currently falls on Sanchez, he expects it to shift toward the People's Party (PP) and Vox soon.
items.title: Citizens Angry With Establishment as Spain Heads to Polls

items.summary:
Young Albanians in Tirana have shifted from leaving the country to demanding political change through a movement they call the 'Flamingo Revolution.' The protests began in May over a luxury resort project tied to Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner before broadening into demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation, electoral reform, and fresh elections.

The unrest stems from domestic grievances rather than foreign orchestration. Protesters cite corruption among ministers and former government officials, rising living costs, and low wages as their driving concerns. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics, half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek—roughly $680—per month after taxes.

The movement has drawn broad support across Albania's political spectrum despite Rama blaming 'foreign hands,' for which there is little evidence. He rejected calls to resign and invited dialogue that protesters have refused so far. The OSCE noted the 2025 parliamentary elections were competitive but took place in a highly polarized environment with reports of intimidation.

The protests reflect deeper frustrations with Albania's party-dominated politics, where seats are allocated by party leaders rather than voters. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes for just one seat, while the Socialists won roughly one seat per 10,000 votes.

The movement also highlights Albania's demographic crisis: its population shrank by nearly 15%, or about 420,000 people between 2011 and 2023, primarily due to emigration. For decades Albanian leaders relied on citizens leaving the country; now students have symbolically burned that luggage.
items.title: Albania's youth protest for reform, not departure

items.summary:
In this special edition of 'How China Engages,' host Wang Guan interviews Vladimir Norov, former secretary-general of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and former foreign minister of Uzbekistan. The discussion centers on whether China is pursuing hegemony or offering an alternative approach to international relations based on mutual respect and cooperation.

The interview addresses growing concerns about China's expanding global influence and questions whether a Thucydides Trap—referring to historical tensions between rising and established powers—is developing as Beijing and Washington navigate their relationship. Norov examines the historical roots of China's engagement with the world rather than accepting these framing assumptions.

Norov outlines the principles underpinning Chinese foreign policy, including non-interference in other countries' affairs, mutual respect, and support for other nations' development. The conversation explores whether these stated principles represent a genuine alternative to conventional power dynamics or simply describe Beijing's self-characterization of its approach.
items.title: China Engages: Wang Guan Discusses Beijing's Foreign Policy With Vladimir Norov

items.summary:
Germany's roughly 3,000 Christmas venues are preparing for an estimated 170 million visits this season as crowds gather across the country.

Munich's Christkindlmarkt traces its origins to the 14th century and offers 138 stalls selling gingerbread, wooden carvings and festive decorations alongside a dedicated nativity market and traditional Krampus celebrations that run until Christmas Eve.

At Cologne Cathedral, more than 140 red-roofed stalls surround a 25-metre fir tree decorated with some 50,000 lights. The market provides traditional crafts, mulled wine and more than 100 free performances through December 23.

Berlin alone hosts more than 80 Christmas markets ranging from torchlit medieval fairs to Alt-Rixdorf's charity weekend event.
items.title: Germany's Christmas markets open amid tight security

items.summary:
The number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training fell below one million for the first time, reaching 959,000 over the three months to September according to the Office for National Statistics. Andy Burnham's government is preparing sweeping welfare reforms after Alan Milburn warned Britain risks losing a generation of young people without radical change.

The drop was driven by a fall in 18- to 24-year-old Neets to 867,000 over the three months to September. However, on an annual basis the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not earning or learning remained 17,000 higher than a year earlier and stays close to its highest level in a decade.

The decline was partly offset by 16- and 17-year-olds finishing education without work or training rising to 92,000, the highest figure since 2012. Overall, one in eight young people were Neet over the three months to September.
items.title: UK Neet Numbers Fall Below a Million as Burnham Pushes Welfare Reform

visual.alt: Bar chart. 18- to 24-year-old Neets 867,000; Total 18- to 24-year-olds 18.

items.summary:
Extreme weather is driving a wave of displacement across Europe as wildfires, droughts and coastal erosion force residents from their homes. The summer's southern France fires were the largest in French history since World War II, burning 42,000 hectares in one week and forcing more than 220,000 people to evacuate.

The European Union has seen more than 700,000 hectares burn this year, including 300,000 in Spain. Suffering from droughts that caused billions in losses and a record-hot summer across much of the continent, Europe nonetheless remains the least-affected region for forced displacement.

A study by Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine estimates more than 50,300 deaths occurred across Europe in 2026, with 65% attributable to climate change. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Center reports that disasters triggered nearly 30 million forced displacements globally last year.

Wildfires account for nine out of every 10 disaster-related displacements in the European Union, according to IDMC analyst Xiao Fen Hernan, who points to lengthening fire seasons and fires moving closer to cities. The center expects EU displacement figures for 2026 to rise sharply from around 125,000 movements recorded in 2025.

There is no consensus on terminology: 'climate-displaced people' covers internal moves while 'environmental migrants' describes cross-border movement, and the term 'climate refugees' remains contested because international law does not recognize climate emergencies as grounds for persecution. Experts say Europeans increasingly see themselves among those forced to leave their homes.

Far from France's fires, coastal erosion threatens Ireland's Portrane village, where rising seas have already swallowed part of a priest's garden and left several homes on the edge of cliffs. Climate Ireland estimates 20% of Irish land is at risk of erosion, while a Council of Europe report found that 25% of European coastlines are eroding.

A study by consulting firm RPS found Portrane's coastline has retreated about 20 meters since mid-century, and projections suggest sea-level rise could put hundreds of homes at risk over the coming decades. Experts debate between building barriers and planned retreat, with some calling coastal relocation inevitable.
items.title: Climate-driven disasters displace thousands across Europe

items.summary:
A working group commissioned by the Irish government has recommended that plug-in solar systems could become legally available to households by mid-2027, provided safety and regulatory reviews proceed as planned. The report was welcomed by Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien, who set up the group to assess technical, standards, safety, regulatory and implementation issues for plug-in technologies rated up to 800 W (AC).

The working group's authors drew on representatives from the utilities regulator, the national standards authority, ESB Networks and O'Brien's department. The distribution operator has backed safe deployment of compliant systems as long as network visibility is maintained through a customer registration process.

Plug-and-play installation emerged as the preferred approach after the group reviewed several options, with its authors noting similarities to markets in the UK and other parts of Europe. They recommended an Ireland-specific safety assessment alongside product requirements, customer guidance and supporting safeguards.

The report warned that product compliance and network compliance are separate but complementary obligations. It also examined plug-in batteries but concluded their international standards were less developed than those for solar, recommending that the initial rollout focus mainly on plug-in systems.

Remuneration for exporting electricity from plug-in solar is being developed as part of the broader plan. O'Brien said the government aims to enable the technology while protecting consumers and supporting a safe, efficient and reliable grid.
items.title: Ireland Targets Plug-in Solar Availability by Mid-2027

items.summary:
The eval bar on chess broadcasts measures what happens between two perfectly playing engines, not who will win a real human game. Patrick Collison argues that viewers actually want to know the current probability of each side winning and how likely a draw is.

HumanFish addresses this gap as an open hybrid model trained on 550,001 tournament positions drawn from 91,720 human games rated between 2400 and 2900 Elo. The training data combines Stockfish 19, Leela Chess Zero, a grandmaster move predictor called DSC-150M, and live tournament clocks.

The model outputs calibrated odds for White winning, the game drawing, and Black winning. It also displays the concrete moves behind each disagreement directly on the board.
items.title: HumanFish Aims to Predict Outcomes of Live Human Chess Games

items.summary:
Washington promised a 100-kilowatt nuclear reactor on the Moon by 2030, but NASA is now bidding for one that produces only 20 kilowatts. The August announcement framed the effort as a race with China and Russia to land a reactor first, which could trigger a 'keep-out zone' around it.

The November bid specification calls for Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) at 20 kilowatts—enough for about 16 American homes—which is one-fifth of the promised size and below even earlier NASA designs. The White House memo on space nuclear power set this minimum in April, pushing the larger reactor into the 2030s without explanation.

The smaller target drew skepticism from experts who said no serious planning had occurred behind the original figure. Katy Huff of the Energy Department found 'no evidence' anyone considered the 100-kilowatt goal beyond it being bigger, and Randy Bell of the Aerospace Corporation called a reactor that size too large to land easily.

LR-1 must survive more than two weeks of darkness at the lunar south pole, keep running after any single failure, operate with minimal Earth contact, and shield astronauts a kilometer away from no more than 5 rem of extra radiation per year. Companies win bids by December 21 for a reactor ready to launch in 2030 that runs five years without maintenance.

Russia and China are aiming later but have not disclosed sizes. Roscosmos chief Yury Borisov said the two countries plan a Moon power plant around 2033-2035, with Lavochkin hired in December 2025 to build one by 2036 alongside state nuclear company Rosatom.

NASA plans $20 billion over seven years for a base near the lunar south pole and will launch its first element in December. The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft is due to fly in 2028 as a design testbed, though it runs at only 20 kilowatts.
items.title: NASA Is Building a 20-Kilowatt Lunar Reactor After Promising 100 Kilowatts

items.summary:
Germany's roughly 3,000 Christmas markets are drawing crowds as they prepare for an estimated 170 million visits this season. The festive venues continue to operate despite heightened security following the deadly attacks in Berlin in 2016 and Magdeburg in 2024.

Munich's Christkindlmarkt, a tradition dating back to the 14th century, features 138 stalls selling gingerbread, wooden carvings and festive decorations. A dedicated nativity market and the traditional Krampus run complement celebrations that continue until Christmas Eve.

At Cologne Cathedral, more than 140 red-roofed stalls surround a 25-metre fir tree decorated with some 50,000 lights. The market offers traditional crafts, mulled wine and more than 100 free performances running until December 23.
items.title: Germany's Christmas Markets Open Amid Tight Security

items.summary:
The Indore Municipal Corporation has cancelled the allotment of 412 houses under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana in Kshipra, Mandar and Tapti residential complexes.

IMC officials say beneficiaries booked these homes through the Indore 311 app but failed to deposit the prescribed amount plus late-payment charges within the deadline despite notices and newspaper advertisements urging them to clear their dues.

Acting on orders from municipal commissioner Kshitij Singhal, the civic body completed the cancellation following the rules. The vacant houses will now be offered to eligible beneficiaries listed in the waiting list on the Indore 311 app.

Beneficiaries who receive notices must submit all required documents and deposit 10% of the prescribed house cost within seven days of getting them.
items.title: Indore Municipal Corporation Cancels Allotment Of 412 PMAY Houses

items.summary:
The National Green Tribunal has flagged gaps in waste treatment and a non-functioning sewage plant, resulting in untreated wastewater being discharged into the Mandakini river at Chitrakoot in Madhya Pradesh.

According to an NGT order, discharging waste directly or through drains into the Mandakini violates provisions of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974.

The regional office of the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board in Satna has issued statutory notices to 103 units including hotels, dharamshalas, guest houses and other establishments. These entities are directed to take corrective action and ensure no untreated water is discharged directly or indirectly into the river.

MPPCB reported that construction on a proposed sewage treatment plant for Chitrakoot town was underway but incomplete as of inspection, so commissioning had not begun.

Because the STP remained non-operational, there were no arrangements to treat wastewater and domestic sewage generated in the municipal area.

During monitoring of the Mandakini river and major drains, water quality analysis results collected during the monsoon season fell within prescribed limits due to the river's self-cleansing property. Nonetheless, untreated sewage continues to be discharged directly into the river.
items.title: NGT Flags Untreated Sewage Discharge Into Mandakini River at Chitrakoot

items.summary:
Mali finished top of Group G at the FIFA U-17 World Cup with a perfect record, beating Vietnam 2-0 on Thursday to complete a three-match winning run and reach the knockout rounds.

Coach Soumaila Coulibaly said Mali had prepared for Belgium, whom he described as a major challenge in their group. Forward Sanaba Keita added that the team focused only on its own performance rather than how difficult each match was.

Supporter Mohamed Cisse credited the new federation with listening to players and fans, saying the country is proud of Mali's performances this tournament.

Côte d'Ivoire also advanced to the round of 32 after defeating Jamaica 3-1. Man of the match Koudougnon Drebo said he was happy to qualify and that his team intended to keep progressing.
items.title: Mali and Côte d'Ivoire Advance to U-17 World Cup Knockout Rounds
